subject: Operating Systems
summary: The operating system is the program that sits between your code and the hardware: it decides which process runs next, hands out memory, mediates every file read and network packet, and stops one buggy program from taking down the rest. Interviewers test OS because it predicts how you will debug real production problems — a service that is slow because of context-switch storms, a worker pool that deadlocks, a container OOM-killed because someone forgot how virtual memory accounting works. None of that is visible from application code alone. Study it mechanism by mechanism: for each one, first name the problem it solves (why), then the design (what), then walk one small numeric example by hand — a scheduling timeline, an address translation, a page-fault count. The sections below follow exactly that order, and the QA bank at the end is the set of questions that appear in almost every OS round, answered the way a strong candidate answers them.

sections.title: 1. What an OS Is: Kernel Mode, User Mode, and System Calls
sections.content:
Start with the problem. A CPU will execute any instruction you feed it, and hardware like the disk and network card will obey anyone who writes to their control registers. If every program could do that directly, one bad pointer in a music player could overwrite your database's memory, and two programs writing to the disk at once would corrupt it. Sharing a machine safely requires a referee with more power than the players.

That referee is the operating system, and the core of it is the kernel — the one program that runs with full hardware access and stays resident in memory the whole time the machine is up. The CPU itself enforces the power difference with privilege modes: in kernel mode every instruction and every memory address is allowed; in user mode (where all your programs run) the dangerous instructions — talking to devices, changing the page table, disabling interrupts — cause a hardware trap (a forced jump into a kernel-defined handler) instead of executing.

So how does your program ever read a file, if user mode cannot touch the disk? It asks the kernel through a system call: a controlled doorway where the CPU switches to kernel mode, but only at an entry point the kernel chose in advance. Your code cannot jump to an arbitrary kernel address; it can only ring the doorbell.

```
user mode                              kernel mode
---------                              -----------
printf("hi")
  -> libc: write(1, "hi", 2)
       -> syscall instruction  ---->   trap handler looks up syscall #1 (write)
          (CPU switches mode)          validates fd 1 and your buffer pointer,
                                       copies 2 bytes to the terminal driver
       <---- return value: 2  <----    return-from-trap (back to user mode)
```

Two numbers worth remembering: a normal function call costs around a nanosecond; a syscall costs on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds to a microsecond, because of the mode switch, register saving, and the kernel-side work. That two-to-three-orders-of-magnitude gap is why high-performance code batches syscalls — reading a file 1 byte per read() call is slow for exactly this reason, and buffered I/O in every language exists to amortize it.

When an interviewer asks "what is the difference between user mode and kernel mode" or "what happens during a system call", they are testing whether you understand that the boundary is enforced by the CPU hardware, not by convention, and that everything your program does to the outside world — files, network, memory allocation, even printing — ultimately funnels through this doorway. Say the words trap, mode switch, and controlled entry point, and give the write() walkthrough above.

sections.title: 2. Processes vs Threads, and the Memory Layout of a Process
sections.content:
The problem: you want to run many programs at once, and you want a crash in one to leave the others standing. The unit of isolation the OS gives you is the process — a running program plus its own private virtual address space (its own view of memory, mapped by the kernel) plus its resources: open file descriptors, environment, user ID, and at least one thread of execution.

Inside a process you often want several things happening at once — a web server handling 50 requests, a game running physics and rendering. Creating 50 processes for that is heavy, so the OS offers the thread: an independent stream of execution inside a process. Each thread has its own registers, its own program counter, and its own stack; everything else — the code, global variables, and the heap — is shared with every other thread in the process. Sharing is the whole point, and also the whole danger (section 5).

Here is the memory layout of one process with two threads. Draw this in interviews; it answers half the follow-up questions before they are asked:

```
high addresses
+------------------------+
|   stack (thread 1)     |  locals, call frames — PRIVATE, grows down
+------------------------+
|   stack (thread 2)     |  every thread gets its own stack
+------------------------+
|      (unused gap)      |
+------------------------+
|         heap           |  malloc / new objects — SHARED, grows up
+------------------------+
|   data (globals)       |  SHARED
+------------------------+
|   text (the code)      |  SHARED, read-only
+------------------------+
low addresses
```

Concrete costs, order-of-magnitude: creating a process with fork() takes on the order of a millisecond even with copy-on-write; creating a thread takes tens of microseconds; switching between threads of the same process is cheaper than switching processes because the address space (and therefore the TLB, section 7) stays valid.

Communication is the other axis. Threads communicate by writing to shared memory — free but racy. Processes cannot see each other's memory at all, so they need IPC (inter-process communication): pipes, sockets, or explicitly created shared-memory segments — more setup, but the kernel-enforced wall means one process corrupting its own heap cannot corrupt yours. That is why Chrome puts each tab in its own process and why Python's multiprocessing exists (section 12).

When the interviewer asks "process vs thread", they are testing whether you can name the exact boundary of sharing: same process, shared heap and globals, private stacks and registers. Candidates who say "threads are lightweight processes" without saying what is shared and what is private have not answered the question.
sections.code:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def worker(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:            # remove this lock and the result becomes unpredictable
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(100_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()

# All four threads incremented the SAME variable — that is what "threads share
# the address space" means. Four separate processes would each have their own
# private copy of counter and each would end at 100_000, not contribute to one total.
assert counter == 400_000, counter
print("threads share memory: counter =", counter)

sections.title: 3. CPU Scheduling: FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, MLFQ — One Worked Timeline
sections.content:
The problem: you have more runnable processes than CPU cores, so someone must decide who runs next. That decision is scheduling, and the metrics that judge it are turnaround time (finish minus arrival), waiting time (time spent runnable but not running), and response time (arrival to first time on the CPU — what makes a UI feel alive).

Work one example through every algorithm. Three jobs arrive at t=0: A needs 24 ms of CPU, B needs 3, C needs 3.

FCFS (first come, first served — run jobs in arrival order to completion) gives:

```
FCFS:   |A.......................|B..|C..|
        0                       24  27  30
waiting: A=0, B=24, C=27 -> average 17
```

B and C wait behind a long job — the convoy effect (short jobs stuck behind a long one, like cars behind a truck). SJF (shortest job first — among the jobs that have arrived, run the one with the shortest next CPU burst to completion; the preemptive variant, SRTF, re-decides on every arrival using least remaining time) fixes it:

```
SJF:    |B..|C..|A.......................|
        0   3   6                       30
waiting: B=0, C=3, A=6 -> average 3
```

SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, but it needs to know burst lengths in advance — which the OS never does — and long jobs can starve (wait forever) if short ones keep arriving. So real systems preempt: Round Robin (give each job a fixed time slice called a quantum, then move it to the back of the queue). With a 4 ms quantum:

```
RR q=4: |A...|B..|C..|A...|A...|A...|A...|A...|
        0    4   7  10   14   18   22   26   30
waiting: A=6, B=4, C=7 -> average 5.67
```

Average waiting is worse than SJF but response time is excellent — everyone gets the CPU within 10 ms. The quantum is a tradeoff: too large and RR degrades into FCFS; too small and you spend all your time context switching (section 4). Typical real values are 1–10 ms against a switch cost of a few microseconds, keeping overhead under about 1%.

MLFQ (multi-level feedback queue — several RR queues at different priorities, where new jobs start at the top and any job that uses its full quantum gets demoted) is how you approximate SJF without knowing burst lengths: interactive jobs that sleep on I/O stay high priority; CPU hogs sink. A periodic priority boost moves everyone back to the top queue so sunk jobs cannot starve. Linux's scheduler (CFS, and EEVDF in newer kernels) is a different design — it picks the task with the least virtual runtime — but the exam-and-interview canon is the four above.

When an interviewer asks you to compare schedulers, they are testing whether you attach each algorithm to the metric it optimizes and the failure mode it carries. Walk the A/B/C timeline; it covers all of that in one picture.

sections.title: 4. Context Switching: What It Costs and Why You Care
sections.content:
The problem behind this section: preemptive scheduling (section 3) only works if the OS can pause a running thread mid-flight and resume it later exactly where it left off, as if nothing happened. The mechanism for that is the context switch — save the CPU state of the current thread (registers, program counter, stack pointer) into its kernel data structure, pick the next thread, load its saved state, and continue.

```
Thread A running
   | timer interrupt fires (or A blocks on I/O / a lock)
   v
[kernel] save A's registers + PC into A's task struct
[kernel] scheduler picks B
[kernel] if B is in a DIFFERENT PROCESS: switch page table
[kernel] load B's registers + PC
   v
Thread B running, unaware it was ever off the CPU
```

The direct cost — the register save/restore and scheduler bookkeeping — is small: roughly 1–2 microseconds on a modern CPU. The number interviewers want you to know about is the indirect cost. While A ran, it filled the CPU caches with its data and the TLB (the cache of virtual-to-physical address translations, section 7) with its mappings. B evicts all of that, and when A comes back it eats a stream of cache and TLB misses rebuilding its state. Measured effective cost is commonly tens of microseconds — 10 to 50x the direct cost — which is why the RR quantum in section 3 is milliseconds, not microseconds: a 3 µs effective switch every 5 ms is 0.06% overhead; every 20 µs it would be 15%.

Two distinctions to state cleanly. First, thread switch vs process switch: switching between threads of the same process keeps the same address space, so the page table is untouched and TLB entries stay valid — cheaper. Switching processes changes the page table, which historically flushed the TLB entirely; modern CPUs tag TLB entries with an ASID (address-space identifier, a small per-process tag) so entries can survive, but the cache pollution remains. Second, voluntary vs involuntary switches: a thread that blocks on I/O or a lock yields voluntarily; a thread evicted by the timer is preempted. A production box showing huge involuntary switch counts (visible in vmstat or pidstat as cs and nvcswch) has more runnable threads than cores — the fix is fewer threads or more cores, not a faster scheduler.

Interview framing: "why are threads cheaper to switch than processes" is really a TLB-and-page-table question, and "why not make the time slice tiny for fairness" is really this section's arithmetic. Answer both with the numbers above and you have demonstrated you understand the cost model, not memorized a slogan.

sections.title: 5. Synchronization: Races, Mutex vs Semaphore vs Condition Variable, Producer-Consumer
sections.content:
Threads share the heap (section 2), and the scheduler can pause a thread between any two instructions (section 4). Put those together and you get the race condition: two threads touching the same data where the result depends on who gets there first. The classic demonstration is that counter += 1 is not one instruction — it is load, add, store — and the scheduler can interleave two threads mid-sequence:

```
counter = 5
Thread A                     Thread B
load counter -> 5
                             load counter -> 5
add 1        -> 6
                             add 1        -> 6
store 6
                             store 6            <- one increment LOST, counter = 6 not 7
```

The section of code that must not be interleaved is the critical section, and you protect it with one of three tools. Know which tool answers which problem:

A mutex (mutual-exclusion lock: at most one thread may hold it, and only the holder may unlock it) answers "only one thread at a time in this critical section." Ownership matters — it enables error checking and priority inheritance (QA 18).

A semaphore (a counter with atomic wait/decrement and signal/increment, where wait blocks when the counter is zero) answers "at most N threads may proceed" — a pool of N database connections is a semaphore with count N. There is no owner: any thread may signal, which is exactly what makes it useful for signaling between threads and also easier to misuse. A binary semaphore looks like a mutex but is not one — no ownership, no inheritance.

A condition variable (a waiting room attached to a mutex: wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; notify wakes sleepers, who re-acquire the mutex before returning) answers "sleep until some condition about shared state becomes true." The iron rule: always wait in a while loop re-checking the condition, never an if — wakeups can be spurious, and another thread can consume the condition between your wakeup and your re-acquiring the lock (Mesa semantics, which every real system uses).

The canonical exam of all three at once is producer-consumer: producers append items to a bounded buffer (fixed capacity), consumers remove them; producers must sleep when the buffer is full, consumers when it is empty.

```
producer --put--> [ # # _ ] --take--> consumer
full?  wait until a slot opens         empty?  wait until an item arrives
after put: notify (waiting consumers)  after take: notify (waiting producers)
```

The runnable version is in this section's code. When an interviewer asks "mutex vs semaphore", they are testing whether you know ownership is the distinction and can name a use case for each; when they ask producer-consumer, they are testing the while-loop rule and whether your notify calls are in the right places. Write the while loop first — it is the line most candidates get wrong.
sections.code:
import threading, collections

CAPACITY, N_ITEMS = 3, 10
buf = collections.deque()
cv = threading.Condition()          # a lock + a waiting room, in one object
consumed = []

def producer():
    for item in range(N_ITEMS):
        with cv:
            while len(buf) == CAPACITY:   # WHILE, never if: re-check after every wakeup
                cv.wait()                 # releases the lock atomically, sleeps
            buf.append(item)
            cv.notify_all()               # wake consumers waiting for an item

def consumer():
    for _ in range(N_ITEMS):
        with cv:
            while not buf:                # buffer empty -> sleep until a producer adds
                cv.wait()
            consumed.append(buf.popleft())
            cv.notify_all()               # wake producers waiting for a free slot

p, c = threading.Thread(target=producer), threading.Thread(target=consumer)
p.start(); c.start(); p.join(); c.join()

assert consumed == list(range(N_ITEMS)), consumed   # nothing lost, nothing duplicated
print('producer-consumer moved', len(consumed), 'items through a', CAPACITY, '-slot buffer')

sections.title: 6. Deadlock: The Four Conditions, and Prevention vs Avoidance vs Detection
sections.content:
Locks solve races and create a new failure: deadlock — a set of threads each waiting for a resource another member of the set holds, so none can ever proceed. The minimal case is two threads and two locks:

```
Thread 1: lock(L1); lock(L2)         Thread 2: lock(L2); lock(L1)

T1 holds L1 --waits for--> L2
                            ^ held by T2 --waits for--> L1  (held by T1)
Cycle: T1 -> L2 -> T2 -> L1 -> T1   ==> nobody moves, forever
```

Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions at once — memorize them, because "name the four conditions" is a direct interview question: (1) mutual exclusion — the resource cannot be shared, one holder at a time; (2) hold and wait — a thread holds one resource while waiting for another; (3) no preemption — the OS cannot forcibly take a held resource back; (4) circular wait — a cycle of threads each waiting on the next. Remove any one and deadlock is impossible.

That gives you the three strategies, in order of how often you will actually use them:

Prevention breaks a condition by design, ahead of time. The workhorse is a global lock ordering — every thread acquires locks in the same fixed order (say, always L1 before L2), which makes a cycle in the wait graph impossible, killing condition 4. This is the answer for real code and the one to lead with. Alternatives: acquire everything at once (kills hold-and-wait, hurts concurrency) or use trylock with backoff (a lock attempt that fails instead of blocking — kills conditions 2/3 at the cost of retry loops and possible livelock).

Avoidance lets the conditions exist but checks every allocation at runtime, granting a request only if the system stays in a safe state — one from which some completion order exists even if every process demands its declared maximum. The canonical algorithm is Banker's: each process declares max needs up front; on each request, tentatively grant it, then try to find an order in which every process could finish (repeatedly find someone whose remaining need fits in the free pool, let it finish, reclaim its holdings). Sketch with 12 units of one resource: P0 holds 5 (max 10), P1 holds 2 (max 4), P2 holds 2 (max 9), 3 free. Remaining needs are 5, 2, 7. P1's 2 fits in 3 — finish it, free becomes 5; P0's 5 fits — free becomes 10; P2's 7 fits. Order P1, P0, P2 exists, so the state is safe. Grant P2 one more unit and needs become 5, 2, 6 with 2 free: after P1 finishes, free is 4 — neither 5 nor 6 fits. Unsafe, so Banker's refuses that grant. Real OSes do not run Banker's (max needs are unknowable), but interviewers ask for the sketch.

Detection and recovery lets deadlock happen, finds cycles in the wait-for graph periodically, and breaks them by killing or rolling back a victim. Databases genuinely do this — that is what a deadlock error from Postgres or MySQL is, with the transaction as the rollback unit.

When the interviewer asks about deadlock, they are testing the four conditions verbatim, then whether you know that industry practice is lock ordering (prevention) while databases use detection. Say both.
sections.code:
def is_safe(available, alloc, need):
    '''Banker's safety check: is there an order in which everyone can finish?'''
    work, done, order = list(available), [False] * len(alloc), []
    progressed = True
    while progressed:
        progressed = False
        for i in range(len(alloc)):
            if not done[i] and all(need[i][r] <= work[r] for r in range(len(work))):
                for r in range(len(work)):        # let i finish, reclaim its holdings
                    work[r] += alloc[i][r]
                done[i] = True
                order.append(i)
                progressed = True
    return all(done), order

# 12 units of one resource type. holdings / declared maximums:
alloc  = [[5], [2], [2]]
maxdem = [[10], [4], [9]]
need = [[maxdem[i][0] - alloc[i][0]] for i in range(3)]
free = [12 - sum(a[0] for a in alloc)]            # 3 free

safe, order = is_safe(free, alloc, need)
assert safe and order == [1, 0, 2]                # P1 -> P0 -> P2 can all finish

# Grant P2 one more unit: now 2 free, P2 still needs 6. No completion order exists.
alloc2 = [[5], [2], [3]]
need2 = [[maxdem[i][0] - alloc2[i][0]] for i in range(3)]
safe2, _ = is_safe([2], alloc2, need2)
assert not safe2                                  # Banker's would refuse this request
print('safe order:', order, '| after risky grant, safe =', safe2)

sections.title: 7. Virtual Memory: Paging, Page Tables, the TLB, and One Address Translation by Hand
sections.content:
Three problems, one mechanism. Problem one: if programs used physical RAM addresses directly, every program would need to know where every other program lives, and a stray pointer could write into anyone's memory. Problem two: loading a program would require one contiguous free region big enough for it. Problem three: you want to run 8 GB of programs on 4 GB of RAM. Virtual memory solves all three: every process gets its own private address space of virtual addresses, and the hardware translates each one to a physical address on every single memory access, using a per-process map maintained by the kernel.

The map is built from pages: the virtual space is cut into fixed-size chunks (4 KB almost everywhere), physical RAM into frames of the same size, and the page table records which frame holds each page — plus permission bits (read/write/execute) and a present bit saying whether the page is in RAM at all.

Translation is bit-slicing, and you should be able to do one by hand. With 4 KB pages, the low 12 bits of an address are the offset within the page (2^12 = 4096) and the rest is the virtual page number (VPN):

```
virtual address 0x2ABC  =  VPN 0x2 | offset 0xABC

page table:  VPN 0 -> frame 5
             VPN 1 -> frame 8
             VPN 2 -> frame 7      <-- our entry
             VPN 3 -> not present (on disk)

physical = frame 7 * 4096 + 0xABC = 0x7ABC
```

If the present bit is clear, the hardware raises a page fault (a trap into the kernel on an unmapped access): the kernel finds the page on disk, picks a frame — evicting someone if RAM is full (section 8) — loads it, fixes the page table, and reruns the faulting instruction. This is demand paging, and it is also how the "8 GB of programs in 4 GB of RAM" trick works: untouched pages live on disk until first use.

Now the performance problem paging creates: the page table lives in memory, so a naive design doubles every memory access (one to read the table, one for the data) — worse with multi-level tables. Multi-level tables exist because a flat one is enormous: 2^20 entries x 4 bytes = 4 MB per process for 32-bit; 64-bit uses four or five levels so that empty regions of a sparse address space cost nothing. Four levels would mean four extra accesses per load. The fix is the TLB (translation lookaside buffer — a small hardware cache, typically 64–1536 entries, mapping VPN directly to frame). A TLB hit costs about a cycle; a miss costs a page-table walk of up to four memory reads, roughly 100+ cycles. With 4 KB pages, 1536 entries cover only about 6 MB of memory — which is why databases and JVMs use huge pages (2 MB) to multiply TLB coverage by 512.

Interview framing: "what happens when your program reads a variable" is the full pipeline in one question — VPN split, TLB lookup, walk on miss, page fault if not present — and they are testing whether you can order those steps and hang a rough cost on each. The worked 0x2ABC example is your anchor; the code below is the same example executable.
sections.code:
PAGE = 4096                                # 4 KB pages -> offset = low 12 bits

page_table = {0: 5, 1: 8, 2: 7, 3: None}   # VPN -> frame; None = present bit clear

def translate(vaddr):
    vpn, offset = divmod(vaddr, PAGE)      # slice the address into VPN | offset
    if vpn not in page_table:
        raise LookupError('segfault: VPN %d not mapped at all' % vpn)
    frame = page_table[vpn]
    if frame is None:
        raise LookupError('page fault: VPN %d is on disk' % vpn)
    return frame * PAGE + offset           # offset is untouched by translation

assert translate(0x2ABC) == 0x7ABC         # the worked example from the prose
assert translate(0x0004) == 5 * PAGE + 4   # VPN 0 -> frame 5
try:
    translate(3 * PAGE)                    # VPN 3: present bit clear
    assert False, 'should have faulted'
except LookupError as e:
    assert 'page fault' in str(e)
print('0x2ABC ->', hex(translate(0x2ABC)))

sections.title: 8. Page Replacement: FIFO, LRU, Clock, and Belady's Anomaly
sections.content:
Demand paging (section 7) eventually fills RAM, and then every page fault forces a choice: which resident page do we evict to disk? Choose badly and you evict a page that is needed again immediately — another fault, another disk trip at around 100 µs (SSD) to 10 ms (spinning disk), against roughly 100 ns for a RAM hit. A 1000x penalty per mistake is why replacement policy matters.

The theoretical best (Belady's OPT) evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future — unimplementable, since it requires the future, but it is the benchmark. Real policies approximate it with the past:

FIFO evicts the page that has been resident longest. Cheap, and wrong in an instructive way: age says nothing about usefulness — your program's main loop may be the oldest page in memory. FIFO also carries a famous pathology, Belady's anomaly: for some reference patterns, giving FIFO more frames produces more faults. The standard demonstration is the reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 — FIFO takes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 faults with 4 (run the code below). It breaks the intuition "more memory always helps," and it happens because the set of pages FIFO holds with k frames is not necessarily a subset of what it holds with k+1.

LRU (least recently used — evict the page untouched for the longest time) bets on temporal locality: what you used recently, you will likely use again. LRU is a stack algorithm — the pages resident with k frames are always a subset of those with k+1 — so it can never show Belady's anomaly. The catch: true LRU needs a timestamp update on every memory access, which hardware will not pay for.

So real kernels run clock (second chance): keep pages in a circle with a hardware-set reference bit that flips to 1 on any access. The clock hand sweeps: bit=1 means clear it and move on (the second chance); bit=0 means the page has not been touched in a full sweep — evict it.

```
        hand
         v
   [A:1][B:0][C:1][D:0]
    A: bit 1 -> clear, advance      -> [A:0][B:0][C:1][D:0]
    B: bit 0 -> EVICT B
```

One bit and a sweep buys a good-enough LRU approximation; Linux's active/inactive list design is a descendant of this idea.

The system-level failure mode to name: thrashing — the sum of working sets (the pages each process actively needs) exceeds RAM, so the machine spends its time servicing faults instead of running code; CPU utilization collapses while the disk saturates. The fixes are admission control (run fewer processes), more RAM, or the modern blunt instrument, the OOM killer. When an interviewer asks about page replacement they are testing three things: why LRU beats FIFO (locality), why hardware cannot do true LRU (per-access cost) and what approximates it (clock), and whether you know Belady's anomaly with the magic reference string.

sections.title: 9. Segmentation vs Paging: Two Answers to the Same Question
sections.content:
Both segmentation and paging answer "how do we map a program's view of memory onto physical RAM?" — they differ in what unit they chop memory into, and every tradeoff follows from that one choice.

Segmentation divides memory the way the programmer thinks: variable-sized segments, one per logical unit — code, globals, heap, stack — each with a base register (where it starts in physical memory) and a limit (its length). A virtual address is segment + offset; hardware checks offset < limit (bounds protection for free) and adds the base. Because segments are meaningful units, you can give each its own permissions and share one — two processes running the same binary can map the same code segment.

Paging divides memory with no regard for meaning: fixed 4 KB pages mapped anywhere, as section 7 described. The program's neat layout is invisible to the mapping; any page can land in any frame.

The decisive difference is fragmentation, so define both kinds inline: external fragmentation is free memory shredded into gaps between allocations — total free space is sufficient but no single gap fits your request; internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated unit. Variable-sized segments cause external fragmentation: after allocating and freeing segments of many sizes, RAM becomes Swiss cheese, and the only cure is compaction (sliding segments together — expensive copying). Fixed-size pages cannot cause external fragmentation at all — every free frame fits every page — at the price of internal fragmentation, on average half a page (2 KB) wasted at the end of each region: a rounding error on modern RAM.

```
                 SEGMENTATION                    PAGING
unit             variable (whole heap, stack)    fixed 4 KB pages
address          segment# + offset               VPN + offset (bit slice)
fragmentation    EXTERNAL (gaps between)         internal (~2 KB per region)
protection unit  per logical segment             per page
sharing          natural (share a segment)       per-page, works fine
table size       tiny (a few segments)           large -> multi-level + TLB
swapping unit    whole segment (big, slow)       single page (fine-grained)
```

History settled the argument: paging won, because external fragmentation and whole-segment swapping hurt more than page tables cost once the TLB existed. x86-64 runs a flat memory model where the segment machinery is vestigial — the FS and GS registers survive as convenient base pointers for thread-local storage — and "segmentation fault" survives purely as the name of the signal you get for touching an unmapped page. Intel's original hybrid (segmentation on top of paging, in 32-bit x86) is a historical footnote worth one sentence in an interview, not five.

When the interviewer asks "paging vs segmentation," they are testing whether you can derive the tradeoffs from fixed-vs-variable sizing rather than recite them — and specifically whether you attach external fragmentation to segmentation and internal to paging without mixing them up, which is the single most common slip on this question.

sections.title: 10. File Systems: Inodes, Directories, and Journaling
sections.content:
The disk gives the OS a numbered array of fixed-size blocks and nothing else. The file system is the layer that turns that into names, files, directories, and permissions — and its two ideas that interviews return to are the inode and the journal.

The inode (index node — a fixed-size on-disk record holding one file's metadata: size, owner, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to the data blocks) is the file. Everything about the file lives there except one thing: its name. Names live in directories, and a directory is itself a file whose contents are name-to-inode-number pairs. That indirection explains a family of Unix behaviors in one stroke:

```
directory "/home/you":            inode 512:                    data blocks:
  report.txt  -> inode 512          size, owner, perms, times     [blk 90][blk 91]...
  backup.txt  -> inode 512          link count: 2
                                    12 direct block pointers
                                    1 single-indirect pointer  -> block of pointers
                                    1 double-indirect pointer  -> pointers to pointers
```

Two names, one inode: that is a hard link, and the inode's link count tracks how many exist. Deleting a file (the unlink syscall) removes a directory entry and decrements the count; the inode and data are freed only when the count reaches zero AND no process holds the file open. So deleting a 10 GB log a process is still writing frees nothing until that process closes it — a genuinely common production incident ("disk full but du can't find it"; lsof +L1 finds the open-but-deleted files). A symlink, by contrast, is a small file containing a path — it can dangle, and it can cross file systems; a hard link can do neither. The direct/indirect pointer scheme is why small files are cheap (a few direct pointers) while huge files pay extra hops.

Journaling answers the crash problem. Appending one block to a file updates at least three structures: the free-block bitmap, the inode, and the data block. Power fails between them and the file system lies to itself — a block marked used that no file owns, or an inode pointing at garbage. The old fix, fsck, scanned the entire disk at boot — hours on modern sizes. A journaling file system (ext4, XFS, APFS, NTFS) uses write-ahead logging: first write a description of the whole batch of changes to the journal (a reserved log area) and mark it committed; only then apply the changes to their real locations; then retire the journal entry. After a crash, replay committed entries and discard uncommitted ones — recovery in seconds, proportional to the journal, not the disk. Default ext4 journals metadata only (data writes can still be partially applied after a crash); full data journaling exists and costs double-writing everything. The same write-ahead-log idea reappears in databases as the WAL — say that in an interview and you have connected two subjects.

When asked "what is an inode," the test is whether you know the name is not in it — and the follow-up about deleting an open file is testing link count plus open count, exactly the mechanism above.

sections.title: 11. I/O: Polling vs Interrupts, and DMA
sections.content:
The problem: devices are slower than the CPU by enormous, varying factors — an NVMe SSD answers in ~100 microseconds, a spinning disk in ~10 milliseconds, a network round trip in ~1–100 ms. A 3 GHz core executes about 300,000 instructions in the time even the SSD takes. How the CPU waits for devices decides how much of the machine you waste.

Option one, polling: the CPU sits in a loop reading the device's status register — "done yet? done yet?" — until it flips. Every loop iteration is a wasted cycle. Polling is the right choice only when the wait is shorter than the alternative's overhead: microsecond-scale device latencies or dedicated cores that have nothing better to do (high-frequency networking with DPDK, io_uring's polling modes, NVMe polling for ultra-low latency).

Option two, interrupts: the CPU starts the I/O, then goes off to run other threads; when the device finishes, it raises a hardware interrupt — an electrical signal that forces the CPU to suspend what it is doing and run the kernel's interrupt handler, which marks the waiting thread runnable. The wait costs nothing; each completion costs an interrupt (a few microseconds of handler plus the cache disturbance from section 4). The failure mode is worth knowing: under a flood of completions — say a NIC receiving a million packets a second — the CPU can spend 100% of its time in interrupt handlers and make no progress; that is receive livelock, and Linux's NAPI answers it by switching from interrupts to polling exactly when load makes polling cheap. The general rule: interrupts for idle-to-moderate load, polling under saturation.

Notification is half the story; the other half is moving the bytes. With programmed I/O, the CPU itself copies data one word at a time between the device and memory — for a 1 MB read that is hundreds of thousands of copy instructions burned. DMA (direct memory access — a dedicated controller that transfers data between device and RAM on its own, telling the CPU when the whole buffer is done) removes the CPU from the data path entirely:

```
1. CPU -> DMA controller: "move 1 MB from disk into RAM at address X"
2. CPU runs other threads               (data flows disk -> RAM without it)
3. DMA controller -> CPU: one interrupt: "buffer complete"
```

One interrupt per buffer instead of per word, and the CPU never touches the payload. Every disk read, network packet, and GPU transfer on your machine moves this way.

Putting the whole read path together — and this is a strong closing answer when an interviewer asks how a file read actually works: read() traps into the kernel (section 1); on a page-cache miss the kernel programs the disk and the DMA controller; the calling thread blocks and the scheduler runs someone else (sections 3–4); the device DMAs the data into a kernel buffer and raises an interrupt; the handler wakes your thread, which copies data to your buffer and returns from the syscall. The question is testing whether you can chain five sections of this subject into one coherent story — interrupts, DMA, scheduling, and syscalls are one pipeline, not four topics.

sections.title: 12. Threads in Practice: User vs Kernel Threads, and Why Python Has a GIL
sections.content:
Everything so far treated "thread" as one thing. In practice there are two layers, and the difference decides what your language's concurrency can actually do.

A kernel thread is one the OS knows about: it has an entry in the scheduler, so the kernel can run it on any core and preempt it. A user-level thread (green thread) exists only inside your process: a runtime library creates it, schedules it, and switches between them in user space with no syscall at all. That makes user threads radically cheaper — nanoseconds to switch and a few KB of stack each, versus microseconds and megabyte-default stacks for kernel threads — which is how Go runs a million goroutines. The catch defines the design space: the kernel cannot see user threads, so if one makes a blocking syscall, the kernel blocks the whole kernel thread carrying it, freezing every user thread multiplexed on it; and user threads on one kernel thread can never use two cores. Real runtimes therefore use M:N mapping (M user threads multiplexed over N kernel threads) and intercept would-be-blocking I/O, converting it into non-blocking calls plus a user-thread switch. Go's runtime does exactly this; async/await in Python and JavaScript is the same idea with the switch points made explicit — an event loop is user-level cooperative scheduling by another name. The 1:1 model (every language thread is a kernel thread) is what C, Java, and Python actually use for their thread APIs.

Which brings us to the GIL. Python threads ARE kernel threads — the OS will happily schedule them on eight cores. But CPython adds the Global Interpreter Lock: one process-wide mutex that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode. Why it exists is a memory-management story: CPython frees objects by reference counting (every object carries a count of references to it; hitting zero frees it immediately), and refcount updates are exactly the load-add-store race from section 5. Guarding every object's count with its own atomic operation was tried and measurably slowed single-threaded code; one big lock kept the common case fast and every C extension's assumptions intact. The consequence: CPU-bound Python threads cannot run in parallel — two threads grinding numbers take as long as one, sometimes longer from lock contention. But the GIL is released around blocking I/O and inside long-running C library calls (numpy, hashing, compression), so I/O-bound thread pools genuinely overlap their waiting.

```
CPU-bound, 2 threads:  |T1 holds GIL....|T2 holds GIL....|   serialized: no speedup
I/O-bound, 2 threads:  |T1: GIL|--waiting on socket-------|
                              |T2: GIL|--waiting on disk--|   overlapped: real speedup
```

The decision table you should say in an interview: CPU-bound Python — multiprocessing (separate processes, separate GILs, true parallelism, pay IPC costs); I/O-bound with thousands of connections — asyncio; I/O-bound with modest counts — threads are fine. And note the ground is shifting: PEP 703 free-threaded builds (Python 3.13+) make the GIL optional by making refcounting thread-safe, trading some single-thread speed for parallelism. When an interviewer asks "why does Python have a GIL," they are testing whether you know it protects refcounting (not your data — your own races still need locks!) and whether you can route each workload type to the right tool.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
interviewQA.a: A process is a running program with its own private virtual address space plus its resources — open file descriptors, environment, user ID. A thread is an execution stream inside a process: it has its own stack, registers, and program counter, but shares the code, global variables, and heap with every other thread in that process. That sharing boundary is the whole answer: threads communicate by writing shared memory (fast, but you now need locks to avoid race conditions), while processes cannot see each other's memory and must use IPC — pipes, sockets, or explicit shared-memory segments. Costs follow the same line: creating a thread takes tens of microseconds versus roughly a millisecond for a process, and switching threads of one process is cheaper because the page table and TLB entries stay valid. Isolation is the flip side — a crash or memory corruption in one thread can take down the whole process, while processes fail independently, which is why browsers isolate tabs into processes.
followUps: When would you deliberately choose processes over threads?
Exactly which parts of memory does each thread have to itself?
Why is switching between two threads of the same process cheaper than switching processes?

interviewQA.q: What are the four conditions required for deadlock, and how do you prevent deadlock in real code?
interviewQA.a: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion (the resource can have only one holder), hold and wait (a thread keeps what it has while waiting for more), no preemption (the system cannot forcibly reclaim a held resource), and circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting for a resource the next one holds). Break any single condition and deadlock is impossible. In real code the standard prevention is a global lock ordering: every thread acquires locks in one agreed order — say, always account-with-lower-ID first — which makes a cycle in the wait graph structurally impossible, eliminating circular wait. Alternatives are acquiring all locks up front (kills hold-and-wait but reduces concurrency) and trylock with timeout and backoff (kills no-preemption but risks livelock). I would also mention that databases take the opposite strategy — detection: they find cycles in the wait-for graph and roll back a victim transaction, which is what a deadlock error from Postgres means.
followUps: Why does a consistent lock ordering make circular wait impossible?
How would you detect a deadlock in a running system you cannot restart?
What is the difference between prevention and avoidance, and where does Banker's algorithm fit?

interviewQA.a: Both map a program's virtual memory onto physical RAM; they differ in the unit. Segmentation uses variable-sized segments matching program structure — code, heap, stack — each with a base and limit register, giving natural per-segment protection and sharing. Paging chops memory into fixed 4 KB pages mapped through a page table, ignoring program structure entirely. Every tradeoff follows from fixed versus variable sizing: segmentation suffers external fragmentation (free memory shredded into gaps between variable-size allocations, so a request fails even though total free space is sufficient) and needs compaction to fix it; paging cannot have external fragmentation — any free frame fits any page — but wastes on average half a page per region as internal fragmentation, about 2 KB, which is negligible. Paging's real costs are big page tables (solved with multi-level tables) and a translation on every access (solved with the TLB). Modern systems settled on paging; x86-64 keeps segments only vestigially, such as FS/GS for thread-local storage.
followUps: Define internal versus external fragmentation, and attach each to the right scheme.
Why did paging win historically?
How does a multi-level page table save memory for sparse address spaces?

interviewQA.q: Walk me through everything that happens when you type ls and press Enter.
interviewQA.a: The terminal delivers the line to the shell, which parses it and searches each directory in PATH until it finds an executable named ls. The shell then calls fork(), creating a child process that is a copy-on-write copy of the shell — pages are shared read-only until someone writes. In the child, exec() replaces the process image: the kernel reads the ELF header, maps the text, data, and stack regions, and invokes the dynamic linker to map shared libraries like libc. Nothing is eagerly loaded — as ls starts running, each first touch of a page triggers a page fault and demand paging pulls it in. ls calls getdents() (a syscall, so a trap into kernel mode) to read directory entries, then write() to file descriptor 1; the terminal renders the bytes. When ls calls exit(), it becomes a zombie — a dead process kept around to hold its exit status — until the shell, which has been blocked in wait(), collects the status and prints the next prompt. The question is testing whether you can chain shell, fork/exec, loading, paging, syscalls, and process teardown into one story.
followUps: Where does PATH searching happen — in the kernel or in the shell?
Why are fork and exec two separate syscalls instead of one spawn call?
What exactly is a zombie process and when does it disappear?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a mutex, a semaphore, and a condition variable?
interviewQA.a: They answer three different questions. A mutex answers 'at most one thread in this critical section': it has an owner, and only the thread that locked it may unlock it — ownership is what enables error checking and priority inheritance. A semaphore is a counter with atomic wait (decrement, block at zero) and signal (increment); it answers 'at most N threads may proceed' — a pool of N connections is a counting semaphore — and it has no owner, so any thread may signal, which makes it usable for cross-thread signaling and also easier to misuse. A binary semaphore superficially resembles a mutex but lacks ownership. A condition variable answers 'sleep until some condition about shared state becomes true': it pairs with a mutex, wait atomically releases that mutex and sleeps, and notify wakes waiters who re-acquire the mutex and re-check the condition. The re-check must be a while loop, never an if, because wakeups can be spurious and another thread can consume the condition first — that while loop is the detail interviewers listen for.
followUps: Why must you re-check a condition variable's predicate in a while loop after waking?
Give a concrete situation where a counting semaphore is the natural tool.
What goes wrong if a thread that is not the owner unlocks a mutex, and why do semaphores allow the equivalent?

interviewQA.q: What is a context switch and what makes it expensive?
interviewQA.a: A context switch is the kernel pausing one thread and resuming another: it saves the current thread's registers and program counter into its task structure, picks the next thread via the scheduler, loads that thread's saved state, and — if the next thread belongs to a different process — switches the page table. The direct cost is small, roughly one to two microseconds of register saving and bookkeeping. The expensive part is indirect: the outgoing thread's data fills the CPU caches and its address translations fill the TLB, and the incoming thread evicts all of it, so the switched-to code runs slow for a while as it rebuilds cache state — measured effective costs are commonly tens of microseconds, ten times the direct cost. This cost model explains two design facts: scheduler time slices are milliseconds, not microseconds, so switching stays under about one percent overhead; and thread switches within one process are cheaper than process switches because the address space and TLB entries remain valid. On a production box, a high involuntary context-switch rate means more runnable threads than cores.
followUps: Why does switching processes historically flush the TLB, and how do ASIDs avoid it?
What is the difference between a voluntary and an involuntary context switch?
How does context-switch cost drive the choice of round-robin quantum?

interviewQA.q: What problem does virtual memory solve?
interviewQA.a: Three problems with one mechanism. Isolation: every process gets a private address space, and the hardware translates every access through a per-process page table, so no stray pointer can reach another process's memory — the mapping makes other processes literally unaddressable. Simplicity of layout: every program can believe it starts at the same addresses and has contiguous memory, while its pages physically scatter across whatever frames are free, so the loader never hunts for one big contiguous hole. Overcommit: because pages load on demand and can be evicted to disk, the sum of all processes' memory can exceed physical RAM — untouched pages cost nothing, and cold pages get swapped out. The costs are a translation on every access, which the TLB caches down to about a cycle in the common case, and page faults, which cost disk latency when memory pressure forces real eviction. It is also the mechanism beneath tricks that look unrelated: memory-mapped files, copy-on-write fork, shared libraries mapped once into many processes, and guard pages that catch stack overflow.
followUps: Walk through what happens on a page fault, step by step.
How can two processes share memory if their address spaces are private?
What is the difference between a page fault and a segmentation fault?

interviewQA.q: What happens on a page fault?
interviewQA.a: The CPU tries to translate a virtual address and finds the page-table entry's present bit clear (or a permission violated), so it raises a trap into the kernel with the faulting address. The kernel classifies it. If the address is not part of any valid mapping, that is a segmentation fault and the process gets SIGSEGV. If the mapping is valid, it is a legitimate page fault: a minor fault when the page is already somewhere in RAM and only bookkeeping is needed — first touch of a demand-zero page, a copy-on-write page needing its private copy, or a page still in the page cache; a major fault when the data must come from disk. For a major fault the kernel picks a free frame — running page replacement to evict a victim if RAM is full, writing it back first if dirty — issues the disk read, blocks the faulting thread, and runs other threads meanwhile. When the DMA transfer completes and the interrupt fires, the kernel updates the page table, marks the thread runnable, and reruns the faulting instruction, which now succeeds. The distinction interviewers probe is minor versus major, because the cost gap is roughly nanoseconds of bookkeeping versus a hundred microseconds or more of disk latency.
followUps: What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?
How does copy-on-write fork rely on page faults to work?
Which page does the kernel evict when RAM is full, and what algorithm approximates that choice?

interviewQA.q: What is the TLB and why is it necessary?
interviewQA.a: The TLB — translation lookaside buffer — is a small hardware cache inside the CPU that maps virtual page numbers straight to physical frames, typically 64 to around 1500 entries. It exists because paging without it would be unusably slow: the page table lives in memory, so every load or store would require extra memory reads to translate its address — and with the four-level page tables that 64-bit systems use, that is up to four additional accesses per reference, a 5x slowdown on all of memory. With the TLB, the common case is a hit costing about one cycle; a miss triggers a hardware page-table walk costing on the order of a hundred cycles or more, then caches the result. Its effectiveness rests on locality — programs touch the same pages repeatedly. Two practical consequences worth naming: process context switches historically flushed the TLB since the mappings belonged to another address space (ASIDs — per-process tags on entries — now soften this), and TLB reach is small: 1500 entries times 4 KB covers only about 6 MB, which is why databases and JVMs use 2 MB huge pages to multiply coverage by 512 and cut TLB misses on large heaps.
followUps: What happens step by step on a TLB miss?
Why do huge pages improve performance for large-memory applications?
Why does a process switch hurt TLB performance more than a thread switch?

interviewQA.q: What is thrashing, and how would you recognize and fix it?
interviewQA.a: Thrashing is the state where the sum of the working sets — the set of pages each running process actively needs — exceeds physical RAM, so processes continuously steal frames from each other and almost every memory access becomes a page fault. The machine's time goes into fault handling and disk traffic instead of useful work, so you see the signature: CPU utilization drops (everyone is blocked on the disk), while disk I/O saturates and the system feels frozen. Adding more load makes it strictly worse, which distinguishes it from ordinary CPU saturation. Recognition in practice: on Linux, sustained nonzero si/so columns in vmstat (pages swapped in and out continuously), major-fault counts climbing in pidstat, and load average high while CPU sits idle. Fixes attack the inequality from both sides: reduce the demand — run fewer processes at once (admission control), shrink heap sizes, fix the memory leak — or raise the supply with more RAM. The kernel's last-ditch mechanism is the OOM killer, which terminates a process outright, and many production teams disable swap entirely so that overload becomes a fast OOM kill rather than a slow thrash.
followUps: What is the working-set model and how does it relate to thrashing?
Why does adding more processes make thrashing worse rather than better?
Why do many server deployments run with swap disabled?

interviewQA.q: What is a race condition? Give an example and the ways to fix it.
interviewQA.a: A race condition is two or more threads accessing shared data concurrently where at least one access is a write, and the final result depends on the interleaving the scheduler happens to choose. The canonical example is counter += 1 from two threads: it compiles to load, add, store, and if both threads load the old value 5 before either stores, both store 6 and one increment is lost — the bug appears only under particular timings, which is why races pass tests and fail in production. Fixes, in the order I would reach for them: make the critical section mutually exclusive with a mutex around the read-modify-write; use a hardware atomic operation (fetch-and-add, or compare-and-swap loops) when the operation is small enough, which avoids blocking entirely; restructure so the data is not shared — per-thread counters aggregated at the end, or message passing where one owner thread serializes all writes; or make the shared data immutable so concurrent reads are harmless. I would also mention detection: tools like ThreadSanitizer and Go's race detector catch races dynamically, because code review alone is unreliable for timing bugs.
followUps: Why is counter += 1 not atomic even though it is one line of source code?
What is compare-and-swap and how does a lock-free counter use it?
How does a race condition differ from a data race, strictly speaking?

interviewQA.q: Explain the producer-consumer problem and how you would implement it correctly.
interviewQA.a: Producers generate items into a shared bounded buffer (fixed capacity); consumers remove them. Correctness needs three guarantees: mutual exclusion on the buffer itself, producers sleeping — not spinning — when the buffer is full, and consumers sleeping when it is empty. The standard implementation is one mutex plus two condition variables: not_full, which producers wait on, and not_empty, which consumers wait on. A producer locks the mutex, and while the buffer is full waits on not_full — wait atomically releases the mutex so consumers can make space; after inserting, it signals not_empty. The consumer mirrors this. Both waits must be while loops, never if, because wakeups can be spurious and another thread of the same role can consume the state between wakeup and lock re-acquisition — that while loop is the classic trap in this question. The semaphore formulation is equivalent and worth mentioning: empty initialized to capacity, full to zero, plus a mutex; producers wait(empty) then post(full). In application code you would reach for a ready-made blocking queue — Python's queue.Queue is exactly this pattern — but interviews want the primitives.
followUps: What breaks if you check the buffer state with an if instead of a while?
When do you need notify_all instead of notify?
Sketch the version with two semaphores and a mutex — what does each semaphore count?

interviewQA.q: What is a system call, and what actually happens during one?
interviewQA.a: A system call is the controlled doorway through which a user-mode program requests a service only the kernel may perform — file I/O, memory mapping, creating processes, network access. User code cannot call kernel functions directly because the CPU enforces privilege modes: in user mode, device access and page-table changes trap rather than execute. The sequence: your library call (say read) places the syscall number and arguments in registers and executes the syscall instruction; the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the one entry point the kernel registered at boot — you ring a doorbell, you do not jump to arbitrary kernel code. The kernel dispatches on the number, validates every argument (pointers are checked against your address space — this validation is a security boundary), performs the work, possibly blocking your thread and scheduling others, then returns to user mode with a result or error code. Cost matters: a syscall runs hundreds of nanoseconds to a microsecond versus about a nanosecond for a function call, which is why buffered I/O exists and why batching interfaces like io_uring were designed to amortize the crossing.
followUps: Why must the kernel validate pointer arguments passed to a syscall?
Why are syscalls so much slower than function calls?
How does the C library relate to syscalls — is printf a system call?

interviewQA.q: Preemptive vs non-preemptive scheduling — and how do you choose a round-robin quantum?
interviewQA.a: Non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling lets a thread run until it blocks or yields voluntarily; preemptive scheduling lets the kernel forcibly take the CPU back on a timer interrupt. Preemption is what every general-purpose OS uses, because cooperation fails open: one CPU-bound loop that never yields freezes everything else, which is exactly what happened on classic Mac OS and Windows 3.x. Cooperative scheduling survives inside processes — an asyncio event loop is cooperative, which is why one handler that blocks stalls every other coroutine. The quantum question is a pure tradeoff calculation and interviewers want the arithmetic: too large, and round robin degrades toward FCFS — response time suffers because a short job can wait behind full quanta of every other job; too small, and context-switch overhead dominates — with an effective switch cost of a few microseconds (register save plus cache and TLB repopulation), a 100-microsecond quantum wastes several percent of the CPU, while a 1–10 millisecond quantum keeps overhead under about one percent. So the rule: quantum large relative to switch cost, small relative to human-perceptible latency; real kernels land in single-digit milliseconds.
followUps: What is the convoy effect and which scheduler suffers it worst?
How does MLFQ get SJF-like behavior without knowing job lengths in advance?
Why does an accidental blocking call inside an event loop stall everything?

interviewQA.q: What does fork() return, what is copy-on-write, and what are zombie and orphan processes?
interviewQA.a: fork() creates a near-identical child process and is the one call that returns twice: the parent receives the child's PID, the child receives 0, and -1 signals failure — code branches on that return value to diverge parent and child behavior. Copying a large process's memory eagerly would make fork absurdly expensive, so the kernel uses copy-on-write: parent and child share all physical pages, marked read-only; the first write by either side traps, and the kernel copies only that one page. This makes fork fast even for a 10 GB process and makes the fork-then-exec idiom cheap, since exec throws the copied image away anyway. On exit, a process becomes a zombie: dead, resources freed, but its entry and exit status are kept until the parent calls wait() to collect it — zombies accumulate when a parent never reaps, and the leak is process-table entries, not memory pages. An orphan is the opposite situation: the parent died first, so the kernel reparents the child to init (PID 1), which dutifully reaps it on exit. This pair is a favorite because it tests whether you know process lifecycle beyond the happy path.
followUps: Why are fork and exec separate calls — what does the gap between them enable?
How do you prevent zombie accumulation in a long-running server that spawns children?
How does copy-on-write interact with page faults?

interviewQA.a: Belady's anomaly is the counterintuitive fact that for some page-replacement algorithms, adding more physical memory can increase the number of page faults. The standard demonstration uses FIFO replacement on the reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5: with 3 frames FIFO takes 9 faults, with 4 frames it takes 10 — more memory, worse result. The cause is that FIFO's eviction choice (oldest resident page) has no relationship to future use, so the set of pages FIFO holds with k frames is not necessarily contained in the set it would hold with k+1 frames; the larger memory can hold a genuinely different, unluckier population of pages. The class of algorithms immune to this are stack algorithms — those where the resident set with k frames is always a subset of the resident set with k+1, for every prefix of every reference string. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms, so for them extra memory can never hurt. The interview point behind the trivia: it is a test of whether you understand that replacement policy quality is about predicting future use, and that FIFO's failure here is structural, not bad luck.
followUps: Why exactly can LRU never exhibit Belady's anomaly?
What is the OPT algorithm and why is it only a benchmark?
Does the clock algorithm behave more like FIFO or like LRU here?

interviewQA.q: Why does Python have a GIL, and when do threads still help despite it?
interviewQA.a: The GIL — global interpreter lock — is a process-wide mutex that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode, so only one thread runs Python code at any instant regardless of core count. It exists because CPython manages memory by reference counting: every object carries a count of references, updated constantly, and those updates are unsynchronized read-modify-write operations — exactly the racing counter increment. Protecting every refcount individually with atomics was tried and measurably slowed single-threaded programs; one global lock kept the overwhelmingly common single-threaded case fast and preserved the assumptions of thousands of C extensions. Consequences: CPU-bound threads gain nothing — two threads grinding numbers serialize on the GIL, sometimes running slower than one thread due to contention. But the interpreter releases the GIL around blocking I/O and inside long C-library calls (numpy, hashing, compression), so I/O-bound thread pools get real overlap. The routing answer: CPU-bound, use multiprocessing — separate processes have separate GILs; massive I/O concurrency, use asyncio; and note PEP 703's free-threaded CPython (3.13+) makes the GIL optional by making refcounting thread-safe. Crucially, the GIL protects the interpreter's internals, not your data — your own compound operations still race and still need locks.
followUps: If the GIL exists, why can two Python threads still corrupt a shared dict-based invariant?
Why does numpy-heavy code sometimes scale across threads despite the GIL?
What does the free-threaded build trade away to remove the GIL?

interviewQA.q: Distinguish deadlock, livelock, and starvation. What is priority inversion?
interviewQA.a: Deadlock: a cycle of threads each blocked waiting for a resource another member holds — nobody runs, ever, without outside intervention. Livelock: the threads are running, not blocked, but their reactions to each other prevent progress — two threads that each grab one lock, detect the conflict, release, retry on the same schedule, and collide forever; the corridor dance where both people sidestep in unison. Retry-with-backoff schemes risk exactly this, and randomized backoff is the standard cure. Starvation: the system as a whole makes progress but one particular thread never gets its turn — a low-priority thread under strict priority scheduling while high-priority work keeps arriving, or a writer starved by a stream of readers on a reader-preferring rwlock; the cure is aging or fair queueing. Priority inversion is the famous composite: a low-priority thread holds a lock the high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread — which needs no lock at all — preempts the low one, indefinitely delaying the high one. This hit the Mars Pathfinder in 1997, resetting the spacecraft repeatedly. The fix is priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily borrows the priority of the highest waiter, so the medium thread can no longer preempt it — and it works only because a mutex has a known owner, which semaphores lack.
followUps: Why does priority inheritance require mutex ownership to implement?
Give a realistic code pattern that produces livelock and how you would break it.
How does aging prevent starvation in priority schedulers?

interviewQA.q: What is an inode, and what happens when you delete a file that another process still has open?
interviewQA.a: An inode is the on-disk record that IS the file: size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count, and the pointers to the data blocks — typically twelve direct pointers plus single, double, and triple indirect pointers so small files stay cheap while huge files remain addressable. The one thing an inode does not contain is the file's name: names live in directories, and a directory is a file of name-to-inode-number entries. Multiple names can point at one inode — hard links — and the inode's link count tracks them. Deletion (the unlink syscall) removes one directory entry and decrements the link count; the inode and its blocks are reclaimed only when the link count is zero AND no process holds the file open. So deleting a 10 GB log file that a running service still has open frees nothing: the name disappears, but the service keeps reading and writing an anonymous file, and df still shows the space used while du cannot find it — a classic production mystery, solved with lsof +L1 and either restarting the process or truncating via its /proc file descriptor. The same mechanism is a feature: open a temp file, unlink it immediately, and you get storage that self-destructs when the process exits.

flashcards.front: Why do CPUs have a user mode and a kernel mode?
flashcards.back: So the hardware itself can stop untrusted programs from touching devices, page tables, and other processes' memory. Dangerous instructions in user mode trap into the kernel instead of executing — the boundary is enforced by the CPU, not by convention.

flashcards.front: What is a system call, in one sentence + cost?
flashcards.back: A controlled entry into kernel mode at a kernel-chosen entry point, used to request privileged work (I/O, memory, processes). Costs ~100 ns-1 us vs ~1 ns for a function call — which is why I/O is buffered and batched.

flashcards.front: Define: process
flashcards.back: A running program with its own private virtual address space plus resources: open file descriptors, environment, user ID, and one or more threads. Kernel-enforced isolation boundary — one process cannot address another's memory.

flashcards.front: Define: thread
flashcards.back: An execution stream inside a process: private stack, registers, and program counter; shares code, globals, and heap with all other threads of that process. Cheap to create (~tens of us) and to switch between.

flashcards.front: Memory layout of a process, bottom to top?
flashcards.back: Text (code, read-only, shared) -> data (globals, shared) -> heap (grows up, shared) -> per-thread stacks (grow down, private). Stacks and registers are per-thread; everything else is common to the process.

flashcards.front: What do threads share vs keep private?
flashcards.back: Shared: code, global variables, heap, open file descriptors. Private: stack, registers, program counter. That boundary is the complete answer to 'process vs thread' sharing questions.

flashcards.front: What is the convoy effect?
flashcards.back: In FCFS scheduling, short jobs stuck waiting behind one long job — like cars behind a truck. Example: bursts 24,3,3 give average wait 17; running short jobs first (SJF) drops it to 3.

flashcards.front: What property makes SJF special, and its two fatal flaws?
flashcards.back: Shortest-job-first is provably optimal for average waiting time. Flaws: it requires knowing burst lengths in advance (the OS never does), and long jobs starve if short jobs keep arriving.

flashcards.front: Round-robin quantum: the tradeoff?
flashcards.back: Too large -> degrades to FCFS, poor response time. Too small -> context-switch overhead dominates (a few us per switch). Real kernels use 1-10 ms so overhead stays under ~1%.

flashcards.front: MLFQ in two sentences?
flashcards.back: Multiple round-robin queues at different priorities: new jobs start on top; using a full quantum demotes you, so CPU hogs sink while interactive jobs stay high. A periodic boost to the top queue prevents starvation. Net effect: SJF-like behavior without knowing job lengths.

flashcards.front: Context switch: direct vs indirect cost?
flashcards.back: Direct: save/restore registers + scheduler bookkeeping, ~1-2 us. Indirect (the big one): the incoming thread evicts the outgoing thread's cache lines and TLB entries, giving an effective cost of tens of us. Thread switches within a process skip the page-table/TLB damage.

flashcards.front: Define: race condition
flashcards.back: Two threads accessing shared data concurrently (at least one writing) where the result depends on interleaving. Canonical case: counter += 1 is load/add/store, so two threads can both read 5 and both store 6, losing an increment.

flashcards.front: Mutex vs semaphore: the one-word difference?
flashcards.back: Ownership. A mutex has a holder and only the holder unlocks it (enables priority inheritance, error checks). A semaphore is a counter any thread may signal — answers 'at most N proceed', not 'one owner at a time'.

flashcards.front: Condition variable: what it does + the iron rule?
flashcards.back: Lets a thread atomically release a mutex and sleep until notified that shared state may have changed. Iron rule: re-check the predicate in a WHILE loop after every wakeup — wakeups are spurious and other threads may consume the condition first.

flashcards.front: Producer-consumer: what does each primitive do?
flashcards.back: Mutex guards the buffer; producers wait on not_full when the buffer is at capacity; consumers wait on not_empty when it is empty; each side notifies the other after acting. Semaphore version: empty=capacity, full=0, plus a mutex.

flashcards.front: The four deadlock (Coffman) conditions?
flashcards.back: 1) Mutual exclusion (one holder at a time). 2) Hold and wait (keep resources while waiting for more). 3) No preemption (resources cannot be forcibly reclaimed). 4) Circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting on the next). All four must hold; break any one to prevent deadlock.

flashcards.front: Which deadlock condition does lock ordering break, and how?
flashcards.back: Circular wait. If every thread acquires locks in one global order (always A before B), a cycle in the wait-for graph is structurally impossible. This is the standard prevention technique in real code.

flashcards.front: Banker's algorithm in two sentences?
flashcards.back: Deadlock avoidance: processes declare maximum needs; a request is granted only if the resulting state is safe — some order exists in which every process could finish even at max demand. Find it by repeatedly 'finishing' any process whose remaining need fits the free pool and reclaiming its holdings.

flashcards.front: Three problems virtual memory solves?
flashcards.back: 1) Isolation — private address spaces make other processes unaddressable. 2) Layout — every program sees clean contiguous memory while pages scatter physically. 3) Overcommit — demand paging + swapping let total program memory exceed RAM.

flashcards.front: Split virtual address 0x2ABC with 4 KB pages; PT maps VPN 2 -> frame 7. Physical?
flashcards.back: Offset = low 12 bits = 0xABC; VPN = 0x2. Physical = frame 7 x 4096 + 0xABC = 0x7ABC. The offset passes through translation unchanged.

flashcards.front: What is the TLB and its hit/miss cost?
flashcards.back: A small hardware cache (~64-1536 entries) mapping virtual page numbers to frames. Hit: ~1 cycle. Miss: hardware walks the multi-level page table — up to 4 extra memory reads, ~100+ cycles. Without it, every memory access would multiply.

flashcards.front: Minor vs major page fault?
flashcards.back: Minor: page is resolvable without disk — demand-zero first touch, copy-on-write copy, or already in page cache; costs bookkeeping. Major: data must be read from disk; costs ~100 us (SSD) to ~10 ms (HDD). The 1000x gap is why replacement policy matters.

flashcards.front: FIFO vs LRU vs clock, one line each?
flashcards.back: FIFO: evict longest-resident page — cheap, ignores usage, suffers Belady's anomaly. LRU: evict least-recently-used — good locality bet, but true LRU needs per-access bookkeeping hardware won't pay. Clock: circle of pages with a reference bit; sweep clears 1s, evicts the first 0 — a cheap LRU approximation kernels actually use.

flashcards.front: Belady's anomaly: what + the magic string?
flashcards.back: With FIFO, more frames can mean MORE faults: reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames, 10 with 4. Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT), where the k-frame resident set is always a subset of the k+1 set, are immune.

flashcards.front: Define: thrashing + its signature
flashcards.back: Working sets of running processes exceed RAM, so the system continuously swaps pages and every process stalls on faults. Signature: CPU utilization LOW while disk I/O saturates; vmstat shows sustained si/so. Fix: fewer processes, less memory demand, or more RAM.

flashcards.front: Internal vs external fragmentation — and which scheme causes which?
flashcards.back: External: free memory shredded into gaps between variable-size allocations — enough total space, no gap fits (segmentation's disease; needs compaction). Internal: wasted space inside a fixed-size unit — on average half a page per region under paging (~2 KB, negligible).

flashcards.front: Segmentation vs paging in one line?
flashcards.back: Segmentation: variable-size, programmer-meaningful units with base+limit — natural sharing/protection, external fragmentation. Paging: fixed 4 KB units — no external fragmentation, needs page tables + TLB. Paging won; x86-64 keeps segments only vestigially (FS/GS).

flashcards.front: What is in an inode — and what is NOT?
flashcards.back: In: size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count, and data-block pointers (12 direct + single/double/triple indirect). NOT in: the file name — names live in directory entries mapping name -> inode number, which is why hard links work.

flashcards.front: When is a deleted file's disk space actually freed?
flashcards.back: Only when the inode's link count is 0 AND no process holds it open. Deleting an open 10 GB log frees nothing until the process closes it — df shows usage du can't find; lsof +L1 locates open-but-deleted files.

flashcards.front: Journaling: the problem and the mechanism?
flashcards.back: One logical file operation touches multiple blocks (bitmap, inode, data); a crash mid-update corrupts the file system. Fix: write-ahead logging — record the whole batch in a journal, commit, then apply in place; after a crash, replay committed entries and drop the rest. Recovery in seconds vs full-disk fsck.

flashcards.front: Polling vs interrupts: when is each right?
flashcards.back: Interrupts: device signals the CPU on completion — right for idle-to-moderate load, wait costs nothing. Polling: CPU loops on the status register — right when waits are ultra-short or under saturation (a flood of interrupts causes receive livelock; Linux NAPI switches to polling under load).

flashcards.front: What is DMA?
flashcards.back: Direct memory access: a dedicated controller moves data between a device and RAM without the CPU copying words. CPU programs the transfer, runs other work, and takes ONE interrupt when the whole buffer completes — vs per-word copying under programmed I/O.

flashcards.front: Why does CPython have a GIL, and when do threads still pay off?
flashcards.back: Reference counting (CPython's memory management) is unsynchronized read-modify-write; per-object atomics slowed single-threaded code, so one global lock protects the interpreter. Threads still help I/O-bound work — the GIL is released during blocking I/O and long C calls (numpy). CPU-bound: use multiprocessing.

flashcards.front: fork() returns... ?
flashcards.back: Twice: the parent gets the child's PID, the child gets 0, and -1 means failure. Memory is copy-on-write — pages shared read-only until first write, so forking even a huge process is fast.

flashcards.front: Zombie vs orphan process?
flashcards.back: Zombie: exited, but its exit status waits for the parent to wait() — leaks process-table entries if never reaped. Orphan: parent died first; the kernel reparents the child to init (PID 1), which reaps it. Prevent zombies: wait/waitpid, SIGCHLD handling, or double-fork.
